FITASC and how international shooting is organised

FITASC is the international federation for hunting-style clay shooting. It writes and updates the rules of Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting; the editions we follow are dated 01/01/2025. Compak® Sporting is also a trade mark protected by FITASC, which is why the name is always written with ®.

The sport is built like a pyramid. Clubs and shooting grounds are at the bottom, national federations above them, and the national federations are members of FITASC. The layouts (groups of stands with their traps) for national competitions are approved by the national federation, those for international competitions by FITASC. A federation may hand an event to a club, but it stays responsible for applying the rules.

What this means for a beginner: at international competitions the FITASC rules are the same in all countries, and many national federations build their own rules on them. National and club events may still use rules of their own, so read the programme of each competition.

At the shooting ground the rules are applied by referees. Each referee holds a certificate from a national federation, and the chief referee needs an international FITASC certificate. At international events, a jury (a small panel of officials) handles protests (formal complaints about a decision), penalties and technical problems.

International competitions come at different levels: Grand Prix events, and continental and world championships. They are usually 200 targets, shot in rounds of 25, over several days. Results are counted three ways: in the open ranking (everyone together), by category (age and gender groups) and by national team.

ClayArena is the platform behind this course. It publishes competition calendars, a glossary and a plain-language summary of the FITASC rules. ClayAway, its service for training tours, is being prepared. Remember: only the official FITASC text counts (it is binding); a summary is a guide, not the rule itself.

Key points

  • FITASC writes the rules of Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting (editions of 01/01/2025).
  • Clubs belong to national federations, and federations to FITASC. A federation approves the layouts for its own competitions; FITASC approves them for international ones.
  • Referees hold national certificates; the chief referee holds a FITASC international one; the jury hears protests.
  • International events use the same FITASC rules; national and club events may have their own, so read the programme.
  • Only the official FITASC text is binding; ClayArena offers a summary.

Did you know?

When a shooter is expelled (sent away from a FITASC competition), this is reported to FITASC headquarters, which keeps it on record for five years.

Stand Talk

  • Coach That's a British term — under FITASC it's a simultaneous double.

    Meaning: The coach switches from British vocabulary to the FITASC name.

  • Coach Ask the chief referee, not the stand referee.

    Meaning: The question is for the senior official of the competition.

  • Referee The jury will decide this one.

    Meaning: The matter goes beyond the stand referee, to the competition jury.

For the interpreter
  • You will translate for referees, the chief referee and the jury, so learn these titles in both languages. The Compak® Sporting rulebook calls the chief referee the Head Referee.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. Who approves the layouts for an international Sporting™ competition?

    1. The local club
    2. The national federation
    3. The referee on the day
    4. FITASC
    Answer

    FITASC

    National layouts are approved by the national federation, international ones by FITASC.

  2. What certificate must the chief referee hold?

    1. An international FITASC certificate
    2. A club membership card, nothing more
    3. A national coaching licence from his club
    4. None: any experienced shooter can do it
    Answer

    An international FITASC certificate

    Stand referees need a national certificate; the chief referee needs an international one from FITASC.

  3. During an argument about a referee's decision, someone shows ClayArena's rules summary. How much does it count?

    1. It counts more than the official FITASC text
    2. It is only a guide; the FITASC text decides
    3. It is binding, but only in Compak® Sporting
    4. It replaces the referee's decision on the stand
    Answer

    It is only a guide; the FITASC text decides

    A summary helps you understand the rules, but the referee and jury apply the official FITASC text.
